title: Sent
tomorrow: who taught you your first prayer, and who will you teach?

cards: Car keys already out, someone checking the game score, a toddler escaping down the aisle. The end of Mass. And the last thing the priest says isn't goodbye.
In the old Latin it's ite, missa est. Pope Benedict the Sixteenth wrote that missa first simply meant a dismissal, and in Christian use came to carry the sense of a mission. Go: you're sent.
Now one man who took that literally. Paul, alone in Athens, walking a city full of temples and statues, waiting for friends to catch up. He stops at a small altar with an inscription on it.

teach.b: Luke tells it in Acts. Paul is invited to speak at the Areopagus, and he doesn't open by telling Athens it's wrong.
He opens with what he saw, in the Douay-Rheims: "I found an altar also, on which was written: To the unknown God." You already reach for this God, he says.

Then he goes wider: God "hath made of one, all mankind, to dwell upon the whole face of the earth." One human family, Athenians included. He even quotes their own poets: "For we are also his offspring."
Only then does he speak about Jesus and the resurrection. And Luke is honest about the result.
Some laughed. Some said, we'll hear you again about this. A few believed, a man named Dionysius and a woman named Damaris among them.
That's the scene the Church means by a missionary disciple.
Pope Francis wrote that every baptized person is one: not a professional, not a salesperson.
Someone who has met something good and is sent to share it, starting from what they hold in common with the person in front of them.
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: Paul's speech to the philosophers of Athens opens with a compliment, a stranger's altar, and a line from a Greek poet.

how: Catholics are sent out at the end of every Mass with a dismissal; the Church speaks of every baptized person as a missionary disciple, sharing the faith in ordinary life.

games.q: your roommate, who isn't religious, asks why you still go to Mass. you're Paul in Athens. where do you start?
o: with what you share: what you both look for.
with the reasons their view doesn't hold up.
with a change of subject, so it stays easy.
games.why: Paul began with the Athenians' own altar and their own poets, and only then spoke of Jesus. some laughed, some wanted more, a few believed.

practice: Open a message to one person you care about, and write one true sentence about something that's given you peace, starting from something you both share. No pitch, no argument.
Send it, save it, or delete it: the writing is the practice.

wordCard.voice: Missionary disciple. Pope Francis's name for every baptized person: someone who met something good and is sent to share it.

orig.note: Latin: go, it is the dismissal. the old closing words of Mass, heard as a sending.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: go, you are sent, the way Paul started at a stranger's altar with what they shared. See you tomorrow.
